name: Day One Biopharmaceuticals, Inc.

profile.description: Day One Biopharmaceuticals was a clinical-stage oncology company focused on developing and commercializing therapies for genomically defined cancers, including pediatric patients. The company's lead product, Ojemda (tovorafenib), was the first approved RAF inhibitor for pediatric low-grade glioma, generating $155.4M in net product revenue in 2025 with 2026 guidance of $225-250M. Day One was acquired by Servier for $21.50 per share ($2.5B enterprise value) in Q2 2026 and subsequently delisted from Nasdaq. This report reflects the company's pre-acquisition profile as of early 2026. Founded in 2018 and formerly headquartered in Brisbane, California.

innovation.label: STRONG
innovation.analysis: Track Record (3/3): Day One achieved a transformative milestone by bringing Ojemda (tovorafenib) from clinical development through FDA approval for pediatric low-grade glioma — the first approved RAF inhibitor for this indication and a landmark treatment for an underserved patient population [1]. The company grew from zero revenue to $155.4M in net product revenue within approximately two years of commercial launch, demonstrating exceptional commercial execution for a small biotech [2]. The successful development and launch of a first-in-class pediatric oncology drug represents the kind of high-impact pivot that defines a company. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI deployment evident. Day One operated as a traditional clinical-stage biotech with conventional drug discovery and development processes. No AI-powered products or internal AI efficiency initiatives were reported [3]. Market Share (2/2): Ojemda was the first and only approved RAF inhibitor for pediatric low-grade glioma at the time of acquisition, giving Day One an effective monopoly in this therapeutic niche [1][2]. The $155.4M revenue figure exceeded expectations for a rare pediatric indication, and the $225-250M 2026 guidance reflected expanding label adoption. Product Pipeline (1/2): Day One was expanding Ojemda into additional RAF-driven cancers, including adult glioma and other solid tumors with RAF pathway alterations. Clinical trials were ongoing for label expansion beyond the initial pediatric LGG indication [1]. However, the pipeline remained narrow, centered on a single molecular mechanism (RAF inhibition) rather than a diversified platform. R&D Intensity (1/1): As a clinical-stage biotech, Day One invested heavily in R&D relative to revenue — the majority of the company's spending was directed toward clinical trials, regulatory submissions, and pipeline expansion, consistent with high R&D intensity for the biotechnology sector [2].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): Day One's name itself encodes its founding purpose — to bring meaningful treatments to patients from 'day one' of their cancer journey, with a particular focus on pediatric patients who have historically been underserved by the pharmaceutical industry [1]. This is a specific, thoughtful mission that directly shaped the company's strategic decisions: choosing to develop a pediatric oncology drug when most biopharma companies avoid the pediatric market due to smaller patient populations and complex regulatory requirements. The mission differentiates Day One from peers and connects its work to a clear human impact. Falls short of a 4 because the company was only 8 years old at acquisition and the mission had not been validated through multi-decade consistency. Community Impact (1/2): Day One's focus on pediatric cancer patients represents an inherently mission-aligned community contribution — developing treatments for children with brain tumors serves one of the most sympathetic and underserved patient populations in oncology [1]. Patient access programs and clinical trial access further extended impact. However, specific charitable giving programs or community foundations beyond the core drug development mission were not identified. Employee Retention (0/2): Small biotech with approximately 200 employees at the time of acquisition. No specific voluntary turnover data, average tenure figures, or employee culture data were available in public sources. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying was identified in available sources prior to the Servier acquisition announcement.

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Infrastructure scoring is severely limited by the stock's delisted status following Servier's $2.5B acquisition in Q2 2026. Most financial metrics are unavailable from standard data sources. Of available data: Revenue growth YoY of approximately 18.6% ($131M in 2024 to $155.4M in 2025) exceeds the 10% target (score 1.0, 1x weight) [2]. The company was in early commercial stage and likely operating at a loss, consistent with a biotech ramping its first approved product — estimated negative profit margin (score 0.0, 1x weight) and negative ROE (score 0.0, 2x weight). D/E was likely low (typical for equity-funded biotech) but exact figures are unavailable. Forward PE, Forward PEG, and 5-year revenue CAGR are not available due to insufficient trading history and delisted status. Estimated infrastructure score of 4 reflects strong revenue growth offset by pre-profit status and limited available data. Pre-acquisition stock price of $21.47 with estimated daily volume of ~800,000 shares provides approximately $17M daily dollar volume, passing the $1M liquidity floor [1][3]. Note: Servier's acquisition at $21.50/share represented a 68% premium, validating the platform value despite the limited financial profile.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): Day One's pharmaceutical business is PROTECTED from AI disruption by multiple structural moats. Drug development requires physical clinical trials, biological testing, and FDA regulatory approval processes that AI cannot bypass — even as AI accelerates drug discovery and target identification, the clinical validation, manufacturing, and commercialization stages remain fundamentally human and physical [1]. Ojemda's FDA approval for pediatric low-grade glioma provides regulatory exclusivity and patent protection that create legal barriers to competition regardless of AI capabilities. The highly specialized nature of pediatric oncology — with complex dosing, unique safety profiles, and small patient populations — further insulates the business from commoditization. However, AI is increasingly accelerating competitor drug discovery timelines and could enable faster development of competing RAF inhibitors or alternative mechanisms for treating pediatric glioma, limiting Day One's monopoly duration. AI Opportunity (0/1): Day One did not generate revenue from AI products or services. While AI tools may have been used internally to support drug discovery research, no specific AI-driven revenue or cost savings were reported [3].

infinite_game.summary: Day One Biopharmaceuticals exhibited a genuine purpose-driven orientation centered on pediatric cancer patients, but the company's brief existence (founded 2018, acquired 2026) and single-product focus limit the evidence available to assess infinite game characteristics. The company's founding mission — bringing treatments to patients from 'day one' — shaped its strategic focus on pediatric oncology, a niche most biopharma companies avoid. However, the Servier acquisition in Q2 2026 ended Day One as an independent company before its infinite game credentials could be tested through market cycles, competitive threats, or leadership transitions. The company scores on purpose and courage but lacks the track record for existential flexibility and worthy rivals.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): Day One's founding purpose — bringing meaningful treatments to underserved cancer patients from 'day one' of diagnosis, with a deliberate focus on pediatric patients — is genuine and distinctive [1]. Choosing to develop pediatric oncology drugs when the commercial opportunity is small and the regulatory path is complex demonstrates that purpose drove strategy. The successful approval and commercialization of Ojemda for pediatric LGG validated the cause through execution. However, with only 8 years of existence before acquisition, the cause was not tested through the kind of multi-decade, crisis-tested consistency that earns a 3.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Day One operated as a small biotech (~200 employees) with the tight-knit culture typical of mission-driven oncology companies where employees are motivated by the patient impact of their work [1]. The company successfully navigated from clinical development through FDA approval and commercial launch, suggesting functional organizational trust and coordination. However, no specific evidence of exceptional trust, employee retention data, or cultural practices was available to assess this dimension beyond industry norms.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No evidence of an infinite competitive mindset was found. As the developer of the first-in-class RAF inhibitor for pediatric LGG, Day One operated without direct competitors in its niche. The company's competitive narrative focused on being first to serve underserved patients rather than learning from rivals' strengths or using competitive pressure for self-improvement. The lack of direct rivals in the narrow pediatric glioma space made the worthy rivals concept difficult to apply.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (0/2): Day One was too young to have faced the test of existential flexibility. The company was founded in 2018, developed a single drug candidate, and was acquired in 2026 before it could demonstrate willingness to reinvent its business model or pivot away from its initial platform [1]. While the company was expanding Ojemda into adult glioma and other RAF-driven cancers, these were incremental label extensions rather than transformative pivots. The Servier acquisition ended the company's independent existence before this dimension could be meaningfully evaluated.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Day One's founding decision to focus on pediatric oncology — a commercially challenging niche with small patient populations, complex dosing, and regulatory hurdles that deter larger companies — demonstrated genuine courage [1]. Rather than pursuing a larger commercial market with higher revenue potential, the founders chose to serve a patient population that most biopharma companies underinvest in. The company then executed successfully through clinical development and commercial launch with limited resources. However, one founding decision, while admirable, does not establish the pattern of courage required for full marks.

investment_thesis: Day One Biopharmaceuticals was acquired by Servier for $21.50 per share ($2.5B enterprise value) in Q2 2026 and is no longer publicly traded. Prior to acquisition, the company demonstrated exceptional clinical and commercial execution — Ojemda (tovorafenib), the first-in-class RAF inhibitor for pediatric low-grade glioma, grew from zero to $155.4M in net product revenue in approximately two years of commercialization, with 2026 guidance of $225-250M [1][2]. The 68% acquisition premium validated Day One's platform value and vindicated the company's contrarian bet on pediatric oncology. The investment thesis at the time centered on monopoly positioning in a growing niche, strong revenue trajectory, and pipeline expansion into adult glioma and other RAF-driven cancers.
thesis_continued: The acquisition by Servier eliminates Day One as an investable opportunity for IOWN. Shareholders received $21.50 per share in cash, representing a 68% premium to the pre-announcement price [1]. For reference, the pre-acquisition bear case centered on single-product concentration risk (Ojemda as sole revenue driver), narrow therapeutic niche (pediatric brain cancer), pre-profit status with limited financial metrics available, and the inherent risk of small biotech companies facing competition from larger pharma companies with more resources. The company's Infrastructure score of 4 reflected these financial limitations — strong revenue growth but negative profitability and insufficient operating history for full financial evaluation. With the stock delisted, this report serves as a historical record rather than an active investment recommendation [3].
key_catalysts: ACQUIRED — Servier completed the acquisition of Day One for $21.50/share ($2.5B) in Q2 2026, delivering a 68% premium to shareholders and ending the company's independent public existence [1]

Pre-acquisition catalyst: Ojemda label expansion into adult glioma and additional RAF-driven cancers represented the primary growth driver, with clinical trials ongoing that could have substantially expanded the addressable market beyond pediatric LGG [1][2]

Pre-acquisition catalyst: Revenue acceleration from $155.4M (2025) toward $225-250M (2026 guidance) demonstrated strong commercial ramp with significant room for penetration growth in the approved pediatric LGG indication [2]
key_risks: ACQUIRED — Stock is delisted and no longer tradeable; this report reflects the pre-acquisition profile for historical reference only [1]

Pre-acquisition risk: Single-product concentration with Ojemda as the sole revenue driver — any safety signal, competitive entry, or label narrowing would have had outsized impact on the company's value [2]

Pre-acquisition risk: Pre-profit financial profile with limited infrastructure metrics — the company was investing heavily in pipeline expansion and commercial buildout, with uncertain timeline to sustained profitability [3]
